delegation.modes.impersonation.label: Impersonation
delegation.modes.impersonation.what: What comes out names the initial identity and nothing else. The service at the far end cannot tell an intermediary was involved, and neither can anybody reading the credential afterwards — which is why the issuer is the only place this is ever visible.
delegation.modes.delegation.label: Delegation
delegation.modes.delegation.what: What comes out CARRIES the chain: an `act` claim, a composite ActAs, or S4U_DELEGATION_INFO in the PAC. The far end can see who is really asking, and can decide differently because of it.
delegation.types.krb5-s4u2self.label: S4U2Self (protocol transition)
delegation.types.krb5-s4u2self.what: A service asked for a ticket TO ITSELF naming a user who was not involved at all — no password, no ticket of theirs, nothing they consented to. It is how a service that authenticated somebody by other means gets a Kerberos identity for them, and it is not a privilege: the ticket is to yourself. [MS-SFU] calls it protocol transition, and it is the one impersonation in a Kerberos chain: the S4U2Proxy hops after it are delegation (#491).
The front end then reached ANOTHER service as that user. Authorized by msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo on the FRONT-END account, which only a domain admin can set, and requiring the evidence ticket to be forwardable. Delegation even when its evidence came from S4U2Self: the ticket carries the chain in the PAC's S4U_DELEGATION_INFO ([MS-SFU] constrained delegation, #491).
delegation.types.krb5-s4u2proxy-rbcd.wha: The same messages, authorized from the opposite direction: msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on the BACK-END account, which whoever controls that object can set themselves. That is the entire security story of RBCD. It needs PA-PAC-OPTIONS, and since the CVE-2020-16996 update ([MS-SFU] 3.2.5.2.3) forwardable evidence too (#492). Delegation, like classic (#491).
delegation.types.krb5-forwarded.label: Forwarded TGT (unconstrained delegation)
delegation.types.krb5-forwarded.what: The client handed over its whole ticket-granting ticket. Whoever holds it can reach ANYTHING as that client until it expires, with no further reference to this KDC — so there is no list of permitted targets, because there is no constraint. The only control is at issue time, and it is on the ACCOUNT being protected (NOT_DELEGATED) rather than on any service.
delegation.types.wstrust-onbehalfof.what: The requester asked for a token ABOUT somebody else. The token names that somebody and does not name the requester, so the relying party sees an ordinary sign-in.
delegation.types.wstrust-actas.label: WS-Trust ActAs (composite)
delegation.types.wstrust-actas.what: The 1.4 addition, and composite by definition: the token is about the named subject AND says the requester is acting. It is the element to reach for when the far end must be able to tell.
delegation.types.oauth-impersonation.wha: A subject_token and no actor_token. What comes back is a token for the subject with no record of who exchanged it.
delegation.types.oauth-delegation.label: Token exchange — delegation
delegation.types.oauth-delegation.what: A subject_token AND an actor_token. What comes back carries an `act` claim naming the actor — and `act` nests, so a second hop appears underneath the first rather than replacing it.
delegation.types.oauth-assertion-grant.w: A trusted party signs a JWT saying who the token is for, and this authorization server issues one. No browser, no password and no consent step: the signature is the whole of the authorization, which is why the issuer must be declared on an application entry as `oauthAssertionIssuer` before any of it is believed.
delegation.types.oauth-saml-assertion-gr: A trusted party signs a SAML 2.0 assertion saying who the token is for, and this authorization server issues one. No browser, no password and no consent step: the XML Signature is the whole of the authorization, which is why the Issuer must be declared on an application entry as `oauthSamlAssertionIssuer` and the certificate registered there before any of it is believed. It is RFC 7523's sibling and NOT the same mechanism — the two profiles hold separate key pairs, and neither can sign for the other.
delegation.types.gnap-impersonation.labe: GNAP grant by user assertion, without interaction
delegation.types.gnap-impersonation.what: A client trusted to skip interaction (gnapSkipInteraction) presented a verified assertion about a person and was issued tokens for them. The person was not asked: the assertion is the whole of their part in it, and the token is theirs with no record of the client in it.
delegation.types.gnap-derivation.label: GNAP token derivation (resource server to downstream)
delegation.types.gnap-derivation.what: A resource server presented a token it was handed and asked for one to reach a downstream resource server as the same person. The derived token carries no more access than the one it came from, and names the deriving resource server in its act chain.
delegation.roles.initial.label: Initial identity
delegation.roles.initial.what: Who the credential is ABOUT. The person who signed in somewhere else, or who never signed in at all — under S4U2Self and OnBehalfOf they were not present and proved nothing.
delegation.roles.intermediary.label: Intermediary
delegation.roles.intermediary.what: Who is acting on their behalf: the front-end service, the requester, the client performing the exchange. This is the party that presented a credential of its own, and under an impersonation it is the party the far end will never see.
delegation.roles.target.label: Target
delegation.roles.target.what: What is being reached — the back-end service, the AppliesTo, the audience or resource. It is an application rather than a person, and it is the layer that decides whether any of this mattered.
delegation.mapKey.param.row0: A person. Something with an entry under ou=users — anybody this service has authenticated, in any of the sixteen families.
delegation.mapKey.param.row1: An application. Something with an entry under ou=applications — an OAuth client, a service provider, a Kerberos service, a WS-Trust relying party.
delegation.mapKey.param.row2: Both, which the middle tier usually is. HTTP/frontend.example.com authenticates (so the funnel files it with the people) AND has tickets issued FOR it (so the registry has it). Two entries, one party.
delegation.mapKey.param.row3: This service, in one trust realm. Every line here exists because it issued or refused a credential. The realm is on the box because a realm is a whole logical copy of this service.
delegation.mapKey.param.row4: The two small lines under a name are different sentences. The first is what the box IS — which of the two stores knows it, or the role its shape was guessed from. The second is the identifier a protocol would have to present to reach it, with that protocol's own word for it: a client_id for OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, an entityID for either SAML profile, a wtrealm for WS-Federation, an AppliesTo for WS-Trust, an SPN for Kerberos. The NAME on the box is what somebody CALLED this thing — a cn, an appName — and is no use in a request you are about to build, which is why the identifier is on the picture and not only in the tooltip. Where the two are the same string only the word is drawn, because the value is already the label; where ONE string is two families' identifier both words are drawn (AppliesTo / entityID); and where the application answers to several DIFFERENT names, the one drawn is the one this act actually carried — or, if the act carried something no identifier attribute holds, the first declared one, with the tooltip saying so. Every name it answers to is in that tooltip either way.
delegation.mapKey.param.row5: A dashed outline is something neither store knows. It is drawn in the shape its ROLE implies and is not an error: an RFC 8693 audience nobody has otherwise mentioned is exactly this.
delegation.mapKey.param.row6: Which way a line goes is at BOTH of its ends. It leaves the box with the round end and arrives at the box with the arrowhead — so the question a reader actually asks, standing at one box: is this line mine, or somebody's on me?, is answered where they are standing rather than at the far end of a curve that crosses three others on the way. Every line here has both marks, and no line here is two-way: two applications that reach each other are drawn as two lines.
delegation.mapKey.param.row7: acts for — an IMPERSONATION. What came out names the initial identity and nothing else, so nothing at the far end can tell an intermediary was involved. Amber because this picture is the only place that fact will ever exist.
delegation.mapKey.param.row8: acts for — a DELEGATION. What came out CARRIES the chain: an act claim, a composite ActAs, S4U_DELEGATION_INFO in the PAC.
delegation.mapKey.param.row9: reaches — the TRUST relationship. What the credential is FOR: the back-end service, the AppliesTo, the audience or resource. The label says whose name it carries.
delegation.mapKey.param.row10: A broken line jumps a party nobody named. A forwarded ticket-granting ticket has no intermediary and cannot have one — the client gives it to whichever service it chooses and this KDC is never told which.
delegation.mapKey.param.row11: may delegate — a CONFIGURED relationship, DASHED until an act has used it. One line per pair an entry allows: appAllowedToDelegateTo on the source (constrained) or appAllowedToActOnBehalfOf on the target (resource-based) — the same controls for the OAuth 2.0 token exchange, WS-Trust and Kerberos. Solid once an act has crossed it. Drawn unless the acts are narrowed by outcome, type or text.
delegation.mapKey.param.row12: Red is a chain nothing was ever issued on. The tooltip carries the KDC's own words for why, which is the same sentence the client was sent.
delegation.mapKey.param.row13: Grey and dashed, from the hexagon: this service ISSUED to that party. It goes to whoever ASKED — the intermediary where a chain has one, the initial identity where it does not.
delegation.mapKey.param.issuance0: Dotted, into the hexagon: this person AUTHENTICATED here. The label is the protocol family and the tooltip is the method — the sign-in screen, an AS-REQ, a UsernameToken, a federated assertion. It is why everything else on the picture was allowed.
delegation.mapKey.param.issuance1: Solid indigo: an ORDINARY GRANT, and the label is the exact one — authorization_code, refresh_token, client_credentials, with the specification section in the tooltip. Out of the PERSON it means a credential naming them went to that application; out of the HEXAGON it means nobody else holds it — a client_credentials token is about the client itself and an X509-SVID has no audience, so the subject and the holder are one box and there is one line rather than two. It takes no amber or green, because impersonation and delegation are properties of a delegation mechanism and a grant claims neither.
delegation.mapKey.param.issuance2: Solid indigo out of an APPLICATION is that same relationship one step further on: what the credential it holds is ADDRESSED to. It is the reaches line above, said about an ordinary grant instead of about a delegation — an access token issued to a web front end and addressed to an API gateway is this service saying the first may reach the second in this person's name, with nothing exchanged to get there. The mechanism on the label is what tells the two apart: a grant, or Token exchange. The audience the token actually carries is in the tooltip, because the box is named after whichever application registered that audience. The line under it names the DELEGATED PERMISSIONS on that token — the values on its scope claim that the resource at the far end has DEFINED, which is what a client asks for by sending the whole permission identifier (the resource's base URI followed by the name) as a scope. default permissions means the token named the resource and asked for none of them: that is what a scope naming the resource's own client_id produces, since that value becomes the audience and comes off the scope claim. It says what was ISSUED and not what was GRANTED — the configured register is the other question, and in development oauth2.delegatedPermissionsEnforced is off by default, so a token can carry a permission its client was never granted (product mode refuses one).
delegation.federationKey.param.box0: The trust realm you are looking at. Every line on the picture starts or ends here, because every relationship is between this realm and somebody else.
delegation.federationKey.param.box1: An application registered HERE whose people are authenticated somewhere else. What points it at a partner is appFederationRelationship on its entry under ou=applications.
delegation.federationKey.param.box2: A FOREIGN SERVICE PROVIDER. It asks this service to authenticate somebody. Dashed, because it is not this service and nothing here can see inside it.
delegation.federationKey.param.box3: A FOREIGN IDENTITY PROVIDER. It authenticates the person and this service consumes what it issues. Dashed for the same reason — and a hexagon rather than a rectangle because it is an identity service, which is what this service is too.
delegation.federationKey.param.line0: Ready — enabled and fully configured. It will work.
delegation.federationKey.param.line1: Disabled — which is how every relationship starts. This is the ordinary state of something somebody has not finished setting up, not a fault.
delegation.federationKey.param.line2: Enabled and NOT configured — the loud one, and it earns being the only red on this page: it will REFUSE at the moment somebody tries to use it, and it looks finished from every angle except this one.
delegation.federationKey.param.line3: A broker that cannot broker — the relationship is fine and the relationship it authenticates THROUGH is not, so the person meets the sign-in screen instead of the partner. That screen checks no password, which is why this is worth a colour of its own: it is the only failure here that produces a working sign-in.
delegation.federationKey.param.noteSumma: An arrow is a REQUEST and not an assertion, which is the one thing about this picture that…
delegation.federationKey.param.note: An arrow is a REQUEST and not an assertion, which is the one thing about this picture that looks backwards until it is said. Everything on the left arrives wanting somebody signed in; everything on the right is asked to do the signing in. So an identity-provider-side relationship — where this service ASSERTS to the partner — points INWARD, because what the partner did was ask. Drawn the other way an identity broker is two arrows leaving the same box with nothing joining them; drawn this way it is one straight line through the middle, which is what a bridge is.
